item.content: When a filter/guard check compares a value to an empty string (e.g. `x == ""`), consider whether the underlying library may return `None` instead; use truthiness (`not x`) to cover both `None` and `""`.

Don't trust type annotations from third-party libraries as runtime guarantees—values annotated `str` may actually be `None`; verify against real logs or library behavior before relying on the annotation.
When fixing a bug caused by a specific falsy value, add parametrized tests covering all relevant falsy variants (e.g. both `""` and `None`) to prevent regressions.

When adding optional sensors/entities that depend on data a device may not report, gate their creation on the value being present (e.g. `if coordinator.data.cpu.load_average is not None`) rather than always creating them, so platforms lacking the data don't get permanently-unknown entities.

When adding new entities to an integration, update all required metadata files together: icons.json (icon per translation_key), strings.json (translation_key -> name), and the test snapshot file (tests/.../snapshots/*.ambr) so entity registry and state snapshots match.
In Home Assistant integrations, secondary/less-important sensors should set `entity_registry_enabled_default=False` so they are disabled by default while still available to users who enable them.

When changing a polling/scan interval constant, update the accompanying comment to reflect the new rationale (e.g. why the old value was chosen and why the new one is safe), rather than leaving a stale comment that contradicts the new value.

In Home Assistant, integration polling intervals are defined as `SCAN_INTERVAL` (a `timedelta`) in the integration's `const.py`; changing it is a one-line edit but the surrounding comment should explain the safety rationale.
Don't leave a comment that justifies the old value after changing a constant—reviewers flag stale/contradictory comments; rewrite the comment to match the new behavior.

When a third-party library changes its data model (e.g. ZoneMinder replacing the `Function` field with `Capturing`/`Analysing`/`Recording`), bump the pinned requirement to the version that supports the new model AND explicitly refresh the object before reading it if the library no longer auto-refreshes on attribute access.

Don't assume a library's read accessor refreshes cached state—when a dependency stops refreshing on attribute read, call the explicit refresh method (e.g. `monitor.update_monitor()`) in each entity's `update()` before reading the value, otherwise sensors/switches show stale data.

When broadening an exception handler to cover an additional error type (e.g. adding `requests.exceptions.Timeout` alongside `ConnectionError`), parametrize the existing test over both error types so each path is verified.

When bumping a dependency version in a Home Assistant integration, update the version in BOTH the integration's manifest.json `requirements` list AND the corresponding entry in requirements_all.txt (generated file) so they stay in sync.

Don't forget that requirements_all.txt is a generated file that must be regenerated/updated alongside manifest.json when changing a pinned dependency version; a manifest-only edit leaves the repo inconsistent.

In Home Assistant core, each integration's pinned dependency versions live in homeassistant/components/<domain>/manifest.json under `requirements`, and are mirrored in the top-level requirements_all.txt (and requirements_test_all.txt for test deps).

When adding device connections (MAC addresses) in a Home Assistant integration, use the `CONNECTION_NETWORK_MAC` constant and `format_mac()` helper from `homeassistant.helpers.device_registry`, and set `_attr_device_info.connections` to a set of `(CONNECTION_NETWORK_MAC, format_mac(mac))` tuples.

When adding new data to a device's `device_info` (e.g. connections, serial_number), update the entity registry snapshot in tests (tests/.../snapshots/*.ambr) to include the new fields, and add the corresponding data to the test fixture (conftest.py) so the snapshot reflects realistic values.

In Home Assistant, device connections are represented as a set of `(connection_type, identifier)` tuples on `DeviceInfo.connections`; network MAC addresses use the `CONNECTION_NETWORK_MAC` (`"mac"`) type and should be normalized with `format_mac()` (lowercase, colon-separated).

When migrating a config entry to a new schema (e.g. replacing CONF_LATITUDE/CONF_LONGITUDE with a CONF_LOCATION dict), bump the config flow VERSION, add an `async_migrate_entry` that moves old keys into the new structure, and update every consumer (unique_id, setup, device_info, config_flow) to read from the new key.

When switching a config flow to a selector like LocationSelector, use `self.add_suggested_values_to_schema(schema, {CONF_LOCATION: {CONF_LATITUDE: ..., CONF_LONGITUDE: ...}})` to prefill defaults instead of per-field `default=` on the schema keys.

Don't forget to update config flow tests and snapshots when changing the config entry version or schema—existing tests that assert on VERSION or on flat latitude/longitude data will fail and must be migrated to the new nested CONF_LOCATION structure.

When migrating a config entry to a nested CONF_LOCATION dict, also update the config flow's unique_id computation to read from the nested keys (e.g. f"{loc[CONF_LATITUDE]},{loc[CONF_LONGITUDE]}") so existing entries keep matching and duplicates are still detected.

Don't forget to update strings.json (and translations) when replacing individual latitude/longitude fields with a single location field—remove the old latitude/longitude data keys and add a `location` key referencing the common location label, otherwise the form shows stale/missing labels.

In Home Assistant, LocationSelector is configured via LocationSelectorConfig(radius=False) for a plain lat/long point (radius=True adds a radius field); it returns a dict with CONF_LATITUDE and CONF_LONGITUDE keys.

When bumping a pinned dependency version, update every place it appears: the integration's manifest.json `requirements`, requirements_all.txt, and any other integration that pins the same package (grep the repo for the package name) so all occurrences stay consistent.

Don't edit only the integration manifest.json when bumping a shared dependency—requirements_all.txt is generated and must be updated too, and other integrations pinning the same package must be bumped in the same change to avoid merge conflicts and inconsistent versions.

In Home Assistant, a single PyPI package (e.g. beautifulsoup4) may be pinned by multiple integrations; a version bump must update each integration's manifest.json requirements plus the mirrored requirements_all.txt entries.

When removing deprecated code (e.g. entity replacement strategies), also remove the now-unused imports and helper functions/classes it depended on (e.g. EntityDomainReplacementStrategy, async_finish_entity_domain_replacements) and any imports only they used, so no dead code or unused imports remain.

Don't leave orphaned helper utilities in a module after removing their only callers—grep for each helper's usages and delete it (plus its now-unused imports) when the deprecation cleanup removes all call sites.

In Home Assistant, deprecated entity migrations are often implemented via a local util like EntityDomainReplacementStrategy + async_finish_entity_domain_replacements that removes old registry entries; once the deprecation window passes, the whole mechanism and its call sites in each platform's async_setup_entry should be deleted.

When tightening type annotations to match SQLAlchemy column types, check whether the column is nullable and widen the annotation accordingly (e.g. `bytes | None`, `float | None`) rather than assuming the annotated type; also add a runtime guard (e.g. `if entity_id is not None`) before passing the value to a function that requires a non-None type.

Don't narrow a function parameter's type (e.g. `Subquery | CompoundSelect` -> `Subquery`) without verifying every caller passes the narrower type; grep for all call sites first, since SQLAlchemy 2.1 type hints may not expose attributes like `.c` on the broader type.

In Home Assistant's recorder, `StatesMeta.metadata_id` is an integer primary key (not a string), so lists of metadata ids should be typed `list[int]`; `StatesMeta.entity_id` is nullable, so filter code must skip rows where it is `None` before calling an entity filter that expects `str`.

When a third-party library is fully mocked in tests, assert the exact constructor/call arguments (e.g. `mock_ec.assert_called_once_with(station_id=..., language=...)`) so a broken mapping or wrong argument goes unnoticed no longer; parametrize over the mapping's inputs/outputs to cover each branch.

Don't place module-level constants (e.g. parametrize param lists) after the functions that use them; put all constants near the top of the module before function definitions for readability, as reviewers flag this.

When parametrizing tests over a mapping (e.g. selector code -> library value), assert all derived outputs together: the library call argument, the stored config value, and any computed unique_id, so a single typo in the mapping fails the test.

When a test asserts on listener/dispatcher counts that depend on how many platforms an integration sets up, update the expected counts and the explanatory comments together when a new platform is added, and check both the pre-reload and post-reload assertions.

Don't assume a test failure means the production code is wrong—when a new platform/feature was added elsewhere, the test's hardcoded expected counts (e.g. number of listeners) may simply be stale and need updating.

In Home Assistant, each platform's async_setup_entry typically registers a new-device listener on a shared signal (e.g. account.signal_device_new) and appends to account.listeners; tests asserting on len(dispatchers[signal]) or len(account.listeners) must be updated whenever a platform is added or removed.

When removing a deprecated platform file (e.g. device_trigger.py), also remove its now-unused constants/helpers from const.py (e.g. TOUCH_GESTURE_TRIGGER_MAP, TOUCH_MODELS) and grep the repo for each to confirm no remaining callers before deleting.

Don't forget to remove the associated repair-issue strings (e.g. the `issues` block in strings.json) and any `async_create_issue` calls when deleting the deprecated feature that raised them, otherwise orphaned translation keys remain.

In Home Assistant, deprecated device triggers are removed by deleting the integration's device_trigger.py, its tests (tests/components/<domain>/test_device_trigger.py), the `device_automation` trigger_type strings, and the deprecation repair issue strings; the replacement is typically an event entity.

When changing a syrupy snapshot serializer (e.g. pytest_homeassistant/syrupy.py) to render a previously-ANY field as a real reference, regenerate ALL affected integration snapshots (grep for the old placeholder like `'via_device_id': <ANY>`) and update each one, since a single serializer change ripples across many tests/components/*/snapshots/*.ambr files.

In Home Assistant's pytest syrupy serializer, device registry entries are serialized via `_serializable_device_registry_entry`; `via_device_id` can be rendered as a `<DeviceEntry identifiers=[...]>` reference by reusing the same `_serializable_device_id` helper used for the entry's own id, falling back to `<ANY>` when the via device can't be resolved and `None` when there is no via device.

Don't assume a snapshot serializer change only affects one integration—after editing the serializer, run the full test suite (or grep all .ambr files for the changed placeholder) to find every snapshot that must be regenerated, otherwise unrelated integration tests fail.

When introducing a StrEnum for state attributes (e.g. InputButtonEntityStateAttribute) in an input helper integration, define it in const.py alongside the existing service enum, replace every use of the generic ATTR_* constant (including in `_unrecorded_attributes` and `extra_state_attributes`), and export it from the package root `__init__.py` `__all__` next to the service enum.

In Home Assistant input helper integrations (input_button, input_boolean, etc.), state attributes are exposed via per-integration StrEnums (e.g. InputButtonEntityStateAttribute with EDITABLE = "editable") defined in const.py and re-exported from the package root, mirroring the pattern used for service enums like InputButtonService.

Don't forget to add the new enum to the package root `__init__.py` imports and `__all__` list when adding a state-attribute enum to an input helper—the issue explicitly requires it be exported next to the service enum, and reviewers/hidden tests check the public export.

When bumping a pinned dependency version, grep the repo for the package name to find every occurrence (manifest.json requirements, requirements_all.txt, requirements_test_all.txt, and any other integration pinning the same package) and update them all in one change.

Don't assume a dependency bump only touches the integration's manifest.json—requirements_all.txt is generated and must be updated too, and the same package may be pinned by other integrations that also need bumping.

In Home Assistant core, a dependency version bump is a two-file change: homeassistant/components/<domain>/manifest.json `requirements` and the mirrored entry in the top-level requirements_all.txt (plus requirements_test_all.txt if it's a test dep).

When replacing generic ATTR_*/SERVICE_* constants with integration-specific enums in tests, grep the test file for every occurrence of each constant and replace all of them (including in `freezer.move_to(...)` and dict-key lookups), then remove the now-unused imports; a partial replacement leaves mixed styles and unused imports that reviewers flag.

Don't leave the old generic constants imported after switching a test file to enums—remove ATTR_*, SERVICE_* imports that are no longer referenced, and verify with a grep that no occurrence remains before finishing.

In Home Assistant, integration-specific enums (e.g. ScheduleService, ScheduleEntityStateAttribute, ScheduleEntityCapabilityAttribute) live in the integration's const.py/services.py and are the preferred way to reference services and attributes in tests instead of the generic homeassistant.const ATTR_*/SERVICE_* constants; EntityStateAttribute in homeassistant.const covers common attributes like friendly_name/editable/icon.

When removing unused constants from an integration's const.py, grep the whole repo (including tests) for each constant first; if only tests reference them, migrate the tests to the integration's enums (e.g. InputDatetimeService, InputDatetimeServiceArgument, InputDatetimeEntityStateAttribute, EntityStateAttribute) before deleting the constants, so nothing is left dangling.

Don't leave a blank double line where removed constants used to be in const.py—after deleting ATTR_* constants, ensure the surrounding blank-line spacing still matches the file's style (one blank line between constant groups).

In Home Assistant input_datetime, the service is `set_datetime` with arguments date/time/datetime/timestamp, exposed as InputDatetimeService.SET and InputDatetimeServiceArgument.{DATE,TIME,DATETIME,TIMESTAMP}; state attributes use InputDatetimeEntityStateAttribute (e.g. EDITABLE) and InputDatetimeEntityCapabilityAttribute, while common attributes like friendly_name come from homeassistant.const.EntityStateAttribute.

When changing a syrupy serializer to render a field conditionally (e.g. `None if x is None else ANY`), verify the snapshot assertion semantics: syrupy's `ANY` matches any value including `None`, so a stored `<ANY>` will still pass against a `None` value—only the reverse (stored `None` vs actual non-None) fails. Update the affected .ambr snapshots to the more specific rendering and confirm the test still passes.

Don't assume a serializer change that makes a placeholder more specific (e.g. `<ANY>` -> `None`) requires regenerating every snapshot—grep the .ambr files for the old placeholder and only update those where the underlying value is actually None; entries with a real config entry keep `<ANY>`.

In Home Assistant's pytest syrupy serializer, `_serializable_entity_registry_entry` renders `config_entry_id` as `<ANY>`; to show a missing config entry, render `None if data.config_entry_id is None else ANY`, since entities created directly in the registry (not via a config entry) have no config_entry_id.

When building a search/catalog over a data source where one entity can appear under multiple aliases (e.g. an integration listed under several brands), deduplicate by the canonical key (domain) keeping the best-ranked match before applying the result limit, so the same item isn't returned twice.

In Home Assistant, the catalog of available integrations/helpers (including uninstalled ones) comes from `async_get_integration_descriptions(hass)`, which returns core/custom dicts keyed by 'integration' and 'helper'; brand entries nest their integrations under an `integrations` key, and only entries with `config_flow` can be set up via a config flow.

When adding a new LLM Tool to the config integration, define it as a `Tool` subclass with name/title/description/annotations/integration/parameters (probatio.Schema) and an `async_call` returning `ToolResult`, then register it in the integration's LLM tool list; resolve the translation language from `llm_context.language` (falling back to `hass.config.language` when it is None or '*').

When adding a new button/entity to an integration that enumerates supported actions (e.g. a StationAction enum), add the new member to the integration's supported-actions tuple in const.py, then update icons.json, strings.json, the test's expected entity list, and the snapshot .ambr file together.

Don't forget to update hardcoded entity-count assertions in other test files (e.g. test_init.py's per-device entity count parametrization) when adding a new entity—the new button increments the count for every device profile that supports it.

In Home Assistant's ecovacs integration, station action buttons are generated from a SUPPORTED_STATION_ACTIONS tuple in const.py listing deebot_client's StationAction members (CLEAN_BASE, DRY_MOP, EMPTY_DUSTBIN, WASH_MOP); each becomes a button with translation_key `station_action_<lowercase>` and a matching icons.json/strings.json entry.

When adding a new supported feature to a lawn_mower (or similar) entity, add the corresponding LawnMowerEntityFeature flag to `_attr_supported_features`, implement the `async_<action>` method delegating to the existing command helper (e.g. `_clean_command(CleanAction.STOP)`), and add a parametrized test case mapping the library command to the HA service (e.g. `MowerTestCase(CleanV2(CleanAction.STOP), SERVICE_STOP)`).

Don't forget to update the entity registry snapshot's `supported_features` integer when adding a feature flag—the bitmask value changes (e.g. 7 -> 15 when adding STOP) and the .ambr snapshot must be regenerated or the test fails.

In Home Assistant's ecovacs integration, lawn mower actions map to deebot_client commands: DOCK -> Charge(), PAUSE -> CleanV2(CleanAction.PAUSE), START_MOWING -> CleanV2(CleanAction.START), and STOP -> CleanV2(CleanAction.STOP) (the same `clean_V2 {act: "stop"}` the vacuum uses); each is exposed as a lawn_mower service (SERVICE_DOCK/PAUSE/START_MOWING/STOP).

When replacing generic SERVICE_*/ATTR_* constants with integration-specific enums in tests, map each constant to the correct enum source: integration-specific attributes to the integration's own StrEnum (e.g. PersonEntityStateAttribute), cross-integration attributes to the owning integration's enum (e.g. DeviceTrackerEntityStateAttribute, TrackerEntityStateAttribute), and truly generic ones (friendly_name, editable, id) to homeassistant.const.EntityStateAttribute.

Don't remove a constant from the package root (e.g. ATTR_SOURCE, ATTR_DEVICE_TRACKERS) while leaving it imported in tests—grep the whole repo for each constant first and migrate every test reference to the appropriate enum before deleting, otherwise imports break.

In Home Assistant, integration service actions are increasingly exposed as per-integration StrEnums (e.g. PersonService.RELOAD = "reload") defined in the integration's services.py and used in async_register_admin_service, while the generic SERVICE_RELOAD re-export from the package root is kept for backward compatibility.

When migrating a test file from generic SERVICE_*/ATTR_* constants to enums, map each constant to the correct enum source: integration service actions to the integration's own service StrEnum (e.g. InputSelectService), service call arguments to the integration's argument enum (e.g. InputSelectServiceArgument), integration-specific state attributes to the integration's state-attribute enum, cross-integration capability attributes to the owning platform's enum (e.g. SelectEntityCapabilityAttribute.OPTIONS), and common attributes (friendly_name, icon, editable) to homeassistant.const.EntityStateAttribute.

candidate.content: Don't leave the old generic constants imported after switching a test file to enums—remove ATTR_*, SERVICE_* imports that are no longer referenced (including ATTR_NAME, which should become CONF_NAME for websocket item keys), and verify with a grep that no occurrence remains before finishing.

item.content: In Home Assistant, the select platform exposes its options list via SelectEntityCapabilityAttribute.OPTIONS (from homeassistant.components.select), while input_select's own service actions/arguments live in InputSelectService and InputSelectServiceArgument in the integration's const.py; common state attributes like friendly_name/icon come from homeassistant.const.EntityStateAttribute.

When adding a new number/entity to the ecovacs integration, add an EcovacsNumberEntityDescription entry with capability_fn reading the deebot_client settings field (e.g. caps.settings.mop_auto_wash_frequency), value_fn, key/translation_key, and appropriate device_class/unit/step, then update icons.json, strings.json, and the test_number.ambr snapshot together.

Don't forget to update the integration's documentation (e.g. the docs repo / integration docs page) when adding a new entity or feature—reviewers explicitly request docs updates alongside the code change.

In Home Assistant's ecovacs integration, deebot_client exposes station settings like mop_auto_wash_frequency as events (MopAutoWashFrequencyEvent) gated by capability flags on caps.settings; new config numbers should be entity_registry_enabled_default=False and use EntityCategory.CONFIG with NumberDeviceClass.DURATION and UnitOfTime.MINUTES for interval-style values.

When adding a new select entity to the ecovacs integration, add an EcovacsSelectEntityDescription with capability_fn reading the deebot_client settings field (e.g. caps.settings.efficiency_mode), current_option_fn/options_fn using get_name_key on the event/type values, key/translation_key, and entity_registry_enabled_default=False with EntityCategory.CONFIG, then update icons.json, strings.json (name + state map), and the test_select.ambr snapshot together.

candidate.content: Don't forget to update the integration documentation when adding a new entity/feature—reviewers explicitly request docs updates (e.g. 'We need to update the docs too') alongside the code change, even when the code itself is correct.

item.content: In Home Assistant's ecovacs integration, deebot_client exposes station settings like efficiency_mode as events (EfficiencyModeEvent with EfficiencyMode values such as STANDARD_MODE/ENERGY_EFFICIENT_MODE) gated by capability flags on caps.settings; new selects should be entity_registry_enabled_default=False and use EntityCategory.CONFIG, with options derived from cap.types via get_name_key.

When adding a new entity to the ecovacs integration whose setter needs different arguments than the default (e.g. auto_empty switch must call `cap.set(enabled, None)` to preserve the frequency set by the auto_empty select), add a `set_fn` callable field to the entity description and route async_turn_on/off through it instead of hardcoding `cap.set(...)`.

candidate.content: Don't forget to update the integration's documentation when adding a new entity/feature—reviewers explicitly request docs updates alongside the code change, and the first attempt is often rejected solely for missing docs.

item.content: In Home Assistant's ecovacs integration, deebot_client exposes station auto-empty as `c.station.auto_empty` (a CapabilitySet gated on the station existing) emitting AutoEmptyEvent; the switch must call `cap.set(enabled, None)` to leave the frequency untouched, unlike the auto_empty select which sets the frequency.

When refactoring a single-item method to delegate to a batch/list method (e.g. async_execute_command -> async_execute_commands), verify the batch method preserves all side effects of the original (error handling, execution registration, refresh callbacks) and pass through any flags like refresh_afterwards explicitly.

Don't leave duplicated logic in a single-item wrapper after delegating to the batch path—move shared comments and side-effect code (e.g. execution registration) into the batch method and remove the now-dead copy from the wrapper.

In Home Assistant's overkiz integration, OverkizExecutor.async_execute_command and async_execute_commands both call coordinator.client.execute_action_group and register executions in coordinator.executions keyed by exec_id; the single-command path can delegate to the batch path by wrapping the command in a one-element list.

In Home Assistant's Axis integration tests, a credential change reloads the config entry; aiohttp's digest auth raises ValueError at setup if the username contains ':' (the password may still contain ':'), so test usernames must avoid ':' while passwords can exercise it.

Don't assume a test failure means production code is wrong—when a dependency (e.g. aiohttp digest auth) rejects an input that a test fixture supplies, fix the fixture (e.g. drop ':' from the username) rather than the integration code.

When a parametrized test fails only for one param id after an unrelated change (e.g. a reload-on-change behavior), inspect that param's inputs against the library's validation rules (e.g. aiohttp rejecting ':' in usernames) and adjust the param while keeping coverage of the special characters in the other field.

When a registry update must move a value from one record to another (e.g. transferring an entity's area_id to its child device), mutate the target record BEFORE firing the registry-updated event so listeners never observe an intermediate state where the value is missing from both records; add a test that captures the target's value inside the event listener to lock in the ordering.

When a validation guard raises on a condition, consider whether the condition can be resolved automatically instead of rejected: if a related record can absorb the offending value (e.g. a child device with no area or the same area taking over the entity's area), do the transfer and only raise when the conflict is genuine (different area, or moving to a main device).

Don't name an internal helper with a vague or awkward name (e.g. `_async_get_child_device_accepting_area`) when reviewers flag it—pick a name that states the precondition and outcome (e.g. `_async_get_child_device_for_area_transfer`), since reviewers may approve anyway but call out the naming as a follow-up.

When adding per-device dynamic sensors (e.g. per-disk read/write rate) alongside aggregate sensors, gate per-device creation on the device reporting the needed data (e.g. `if disk.io_counters is None: return []`), set `entity_registry_enabled_default=False`, and reuse the existing dynamic-device listener (e.g. the network-interface listener) to add sensors for devices that appear later.

candidate.content: When adding new sensor descriptions to an integration, update icons.json (icon per translation_key), strings.json (name per translation_key, including translation_placeholders like `{disk}`), and the test snapshot .ambr file together so entity registry and state snapshots match.
Don't forget to update the integration's documentation when adding new sensors/entities—reviewers request docs updates alongside the code change.

item.content: When a config flow step reads a key from an existing config entry (e.g. `reconfigure_entry.data[CONF_PORT]`), use `.get(key, DEFAULT)` with the integration's default constant so legacy entries created before the key existed can still be reconfigured instead of raising KeyError.

Don't assume every config entry contains every key currently defined in the flow—entries created by older versions may lack newer keys; use `.get()` with a sensible default when prefilling reconfigure/options forms.

When fixing a legacy-entry compatibility bug, add a test that builds a MockConfigEntry with only the old keys (omitting the new one) and asserts the flow still produces a form with the expected default, rather than only testing entries with the full current schema.

When bumping a dependency that has a transitive/companion requirement (e.g. modbus-connection[tmodbus] requires a specific tmodbus version), bump both packages together in the same change and verify the pinned versions are mutually compatible per the release notes.

Don't bump only the primary package when its extra/companion dependency (e.g. tmodbus required by modbus-connection[tmodbus]) also needs a version change—update both manifest.json requirements and both mirrored requirements_all.txt entries.

In Home Assistant's modbus integration, manifest.json pins pymodbus, modbus-connection[tmodbus], and tmodbus; modbus-connection's tmodbus extra requires a matching tmodbus version, so the two must be bumped in lockstep and both mirrored in requirements_all.txt.

When bumping a dependency whose release notes say the breaking changes are library-internal only (private attributes removed) and the integration already uses the public API, verify by grepping the integration and its tests for the removed private symbols before assuming no code changes are needed; the change may legitimately be just the two version files.

Don't over-edit when a dependency bump's release notes state the integration code and tests are unaffected—resist touching integration code or tests just to 'look busy'; the correct diff may be only manifest.json and requirements_all.txt.

In Home Assistant's unifiprotect integration, uiprotect is pinned in homeassistant/components/unifiprotect/manifest.json `requirements` and mirrored in requirements_all.txt; uiprotect 25.0.0 removed private camera setting mirrors (HDR, video mode, OSD, LCD message, detection switches, high FPS) and private chime ring settings, but the integration already uses the public API so no code changes are required.

When entity creation is gated on whether a device reports a value, prefer deriving support from the device's static metadata/feature declarations (e.g. a `features` mapping of feature -> instances -> sensor_keys) rather than from the current sensor-value payload, so entities are created for all supported capabilities even before a value has been reported.

When adding a helper that aggregates supported keys across nested feature/instance mappings, add a test fixture device that declares multiple instances of the same feature (e.g. several `range` instances mapping to different sensor keys) so the flattening logic and per-key entity creation are exercised.

Don't leave test fixture devices with empty `features={}` when the production code now reads from features to decide entity creation—populate each fixture's features to match the sensors it is expected to expose, otherwise the new gating logic silently creates no entities and tests pass vacuously.

When adding a per-view limit/option to a base view class (e.g. `max_body_size` on HomeAssistantView), apply it in the shared request handler factory BEFORE the handler and its decorators (e.g. RequestDataValidator) run, so decorators that read the body are also covered; then set the attribute on each affected view subclass.

Don't limit only the endpoints named in the issue title—audit all unauthenticated views (e.g. onboarding user creation, wait-for-integration, backup restore) and apply the same limit, while leaving genuinely large uploads (e.g. onboarding backup upload) at the default limit.

In Home Assistant, the global aiohttp request body limit is 16 MiB (set for Supervisor proxy/ingress/audio-video) and the WebSocket auth message uses aiohttp's 4 MiB default; unauthenticated auth endpoints only need a few KB, so a shared constant like MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED_BODY_SIZE (64 KiB) in components/http/const.py is used for both HTTP views and the websocket auth-phase message length check.

When migrating a sub-device (via_device_id) to a ChildDeviceInfo (parent_device_id), keep the same device identifiers so existing entities and user customizations are preserved, and replace the manually-built name/model/manufacturer/configuration_url with a translation_key + translation_placeholders entry in strings.json under a top-level `device` block.

Don't leave stale comments claiming the integration creates no child devices after introducing ChildDeviceInfo—update comments in async_remove_config_entry_device and setup ordering (e.g. 'ensure parent devices are set up before their child devices') to match the new parent/child relationship.

In Home Assistant, ChildDeviceInfo (from homeassistant.helpers.device_registry) replaces via_device_id with parent_device_id and inherits name/model/manufacturer from the parent; child device names are localized via a `device` section in strings.json (e.g. "device": {"lens": {"name": "Lens {lens}"}}) referenced by translation_key/translation_placeholders.

In Home Assistant's gh-aw workflows (.github/workflows/*.md), the compiled *.lock.yml is auto-generated and must be regenerated (not hand-edited) after changing the source .md; the lock file's gh-aw-metadata header (body_hash) changes accordingly.

When editing a gh-aw workflow prompt (.github/workflows/*.md), change only the instruction text and regenerate the corresponding .lock.yml so its body_hash matches; keep the diff minimal and do not touch unrelated generated metadata.
Don't hand-edit a gh-aw *.lock.yml file's body—it is generated from the sibling .md; edit the .md and regenerate the lock file so the metadata body_hash stays consistent.

When a dependency bump splits a library into new packages (e.g. universal-silabs-flasher 1.2.0 spinning out pygbl and aiospinel), add the new package(s) to the integration's manifest.json requirements AND requirements_all.txt, update imports to the new module, and update test patch targets to the new module path.

Don't forget to add newly split-out library loggers (e.g. aiospinel) to the `loggers` list in every integration manifest that previously listed the parent library (e.g. universal_silabs_flasher), otherwise debug logging for those integrations silently loses the moved subsystem's traffic.

When a config flow starts a background task that may complete synchronously (e.g. via eager_start), pass `eager_start=False` and set any state the task's error path needs (e.g. installing_firmware_name) before creating the task, so the progress step is always shown and tests aren't flaky depending on module import state.

When adding error handling that marks an entity unavailable, follow the log-when-unavailable pattern: log at info level only on the transition to unavailable (guard with `if self._attr_available:`), set `_attr_available = False`, and log again at info when it recovers (check `if not self._attr_available` after a successful update).

When adding tests to an integration that previously had none, create tests/components/<domain>/__init__.py and add the test directory to CODEOWNERS next to the integration's existing entry so the new tests are owned and reviewed.

Don't catch only the library's specific exception type when a request-based library can also raise requests exceptions (e.g. ConnectionError, Timeout); catch both `COOPSAPIError` and `requests.exceptions.RequestException` so network failures don't produce unhandled tracebacks.

When a per-entity value (e.g. min/max/step) comes from static device-reported capabilities rather than live state, prefer a dedicated entity subclass that sets the `_attr_*` values in `__init__` from the device model, and select it in async_setup_entry by description key, instead of reading the values dynamically through properties on every access.

Don't read static capability values (e.g. a boiler's target_temperature_min/max/step) dynamically via properties when they never change—reviewers prefer setting them once in the entity constructor into `_attr_native_min_value`/`_attr_native_max_value`/`_attr_native_step` via a subclass.

In Home Assistant's lamarzocco integration, pylamarzocco's CoffeeBoiler model (from dashboard.config[WidgetType.CM_COFFEE_BOILER]) exposes target_temperature_min, target_temperature_max and target_temperature_step, which differ per machine (e.g. Linea Micra 80–100°C, GS3 80–110°C, both 0.1°C step); these should drive the coffee_temp number entity's native min/max/step instead of a fixed 85–104°C range.

When an entity shows no name because its translation_key has no matching entry in strings.json, grep strings.json for the key and for near-miss keys (e.g. `resume` vs `resume_all`) to find the mismatch, then rename the strings.json key to match the code rather than changing the code, so existing entity unique_ids/entity_ids are preserved.

Don't assume a missing entity name is a code bug—check whether the translation_key used in the platform file actually exists in strings.json; a key defined but unused (e.g. `resume_all`) is a strong signal the code and strings drifted apart.

In Home Assistant, an entity's entity_id and friendly_name are derived from the translation_key's `name` in strings.json when `has_entity_name` is True; adding/fixing that name changes the entity_id (e.g. `button.vm_web` -> `button.vm_web_resume`) and the friendly name (`vm-web` -> `vm-web Resume`), so the entity registry and state snapshots must be regenerated.

When a dependency bump adds a new capability (e.g. RELEASE_NOTES support), implement the corresponding entity method (e.g. async_release_notes) and add the feature flag to _attr_supported_features, then extend the test fixtures with the new library data structures (e.g. ChangelogEntry tuples) so the new code path is exercised.

Don't pass a parsed/normalized version to a library helper that matches against raw changelog version strings (e.g. OpenThread versions with `SL-OPENTHREAD/` prefix and `_GitHub-<hash>` suffix)—use the raw firmware_version string instead, otherwise no changelog entries match.

In Home Assistant's homeassistant_hardware integration, ha-silabs-firmware-client is pinned in manifest.json requirements and mirrored in requirements_all.txt; version 0.4.0 adds ChangelogEntry/changelogs and FirmwareMetadata.release_notes_since(version) for concatenating intermediate changelog entries.

In Home Assistant, LocationSelectorConfig(radius=True) returns a dict with CONF_LATITUDE, CONF_LONGITUDE, and CONF_RADIUS, where CONF_RADIUS is in meters; when the underlying API expects kilometers (e.g. aiopurpleair's nearby-sensors distance), divide by 1000 and set the default radius constant in meters (e.g. DEFAULT_DISTANCE = 5000).

When replacing separate latitude/longitude/distance fields with a single LocationSelector(radius=True), read the radius with `location.get(CONF_RADIUS, DEFAULT)` so submissions without a radius still work, and prefill the form via `self.add_suggested_values_to_schema(schema, {CONF_LOCATION: {CONF_LATITUDE: ..., CONF_LONGITUDE: ..., CONF_RADIUS: ...}})` using hass.config defaults.

Don't forget to update the config flow tests and snapshots when switching to LocationSelector—existing tests that submit flat CONF_LATITUDE/CONF_LONGITUDE/CONF_DISTANCE keys must be migrated to a nested CONF_LOCATION dict (with CONF_RADIUS in meters), and any form-schema assertions must reflect the new selector.

In Home Assistant, each integration can have a homeassistant/components/<domain>/quality_scale.yaml listing every quality-scale rule under `rules:` with a `status` (done/todo/exempt) and an optional `comment`; rules are grouped by tier (Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum) with comments, and rules that don't apply use `status: exempt` with a reason.

When writing a quality_scale.yaml assessment, ground each `todo` comment in concrete code evidence (file/function names, specific missing branches, exact strings.json keys) and cross-reference related rules (e.g. note that action-exceptions overlaps action-setup) rather than writing generic advice.

Don't mark a quality-scale rule `done` without checking the actual code path—e.g. verify PARALLEL_UPDATES is set per platform, that entities raise HomeAssistantError/ServiceValidationError instead of library exceptions, and that config flow unique IDs use a stable device identifier (UUID) rather than host/IP.

When wrapping a resource (file/stream/connection) in a helper that must close it on early termination, provide both a synchronous `close`/`abort` callback (for garbage collection / non-async cleanup) and an async `aclose` callback, and guard against close-during-open by setting a `_closed` flag checked after the open completes so a connection opened after an abort is immediately torn down.

Don't leave the open sequence unguarded when a resource can be aborted concurrently: wrap the open calls in try/finally and check the closed flag in the finally block (calling abort if closed) so a connection created after an abort is not leaked.

In Home Assistant, `homeassistant.util.async_iterator.ResourceChunkIterator` wraps a `read` coroutine plus `close`/`aclose` callbacks into an async iterator that closes the underlying resource when fully read, on read failure, on explicit close, or on garbage collection—use it instead of hand-rolled async file iterators so early-terminated streams release their connection.

When removing a deprecated compatibility mapping (e.g. a legacy effect/state value mapped to a new one), remove the whole deprecation apparatus together: the mapping constant, the compatibility branch, the repair issue creation call, the issue strings in strings.json, and the test that covered the deprecated path—then grep for the removed constant and translation_key to confirm no references remain.

Don't leave imports that were only used by the removed deprecation code (e.g. async_create_issue, IssueSeverity, DOMAIN, ATTR_EFFECT, SERVICE_TURN_ON, LIGHT_DOMAIN, issue_registry fixture) after deleting the deprecated branch and its test—remove them so no unused imports remain.

In Home Assistant's hue integration, the deprecated effect "None" was replaced by the light platform's EFFECT_OFF ("off") in HA 2025.4 with breaks_in_ha_version 2025.10; the compatibility mapping lived in v2/light.py's async_turn_on and raised a `deprecated_effect_none` repair issue defined in strings.json under `issues`.

When marking an integration's quality scale (e.g. bronze) in manifest.json, also remove the integration's domain from the corresponding exclusion list in script/hassfest/quality_scale.py (e.g. the list of integrations without a quality scale), otherwise hassfest validation fails.

Don't end a config flow test on an abort result when the test is meant to exercise a form error path—continue the flow to a success result so the error-handling branch is actually verified; abort is only a valid terminal assertion for flows that genuinely abort.

In Home Assistant, an integration's quality scale tier is declared via the `quality_scale` key in its manifest.json (e.g. "quality_scale": "bronze"), and hassfest's script/hassfest/quality_scale.py maintains exclusion lists of integrations that don't yet meet a tier.

When bumping an integration's quality scale tier (e.g. bronze -> silver), verify every rule in the target tier is marked done or exempt in quality_scale.yaml before changing the manifest, then update the manifest's `quality_scale` key and remove the domain from the corresponding exclusion list in script/hassfest/quality_scale.py.

Don't bump the declared quality_scale in manifest.json while leaving the integration in hassfest's exclusion list for that tier (script/hassfest/quality_scale.py) or while any rule in the target tier is still `todo`—hassfest validation will fail.

In Home Assistant, a quality-scale tier bump is a metadata-only change: the tier is declared via the `quality_scale` key in homeassistant/components/<domain>/manifest.json, and the integration must be removed from the matching exclusion list in script/hassfest/quality_scale.py; no runtime code changes are needed.

When adding an optional sensor gated on a device-reported value (e.g. humidity that reads 0 on models without the sensor), add an `exists_fn` field to the entity description (defaulting to `lambda _: True`) and filter descriptions in async_setup_entry with `if description.exists_fn(coordinator.data)`, so the entity is only created on units that actually report the capability.

Don't gate entity creation on a live value read only at setup without noting the tradeoff: if the library maps a property-access error to 0 (or the value is transiently absent), exists_fn will skip the entity until the integration is reloaded. Prefer static capability/feature metadata when available, and add a test for the initial-read-error case.

In Home Assistant's flexit_bacnet integration, sensors are defined as FlexitSensorEntityDescription entries in sensor.py with key/device_class/state_class/native_unit_of_measurement/translation_key/value_fn; the library exposes extract_air_humidity (BACnet AI96, relative humidity in %) only on models with a built-in humidity sensor, reporting 0 otherwise.

In Home Assistant's DataUpdateCoordinator, `retry_after` from UpdateFailed REPLACES the configured update interval rather than extending it, so a rate-limit backoff can make a slow-polling hub poll faster; floor it with `max(retry_after, self._default_update_interval)` when the backoff must never speed up polling.

When fixing a coordinator backoff that must not shorten the configured interval, write a test that ticks the full configured interval, triggers the rate-limit error, then advances only the retry_after and asserts no refresh happened, and finally advances the remainder of the configured interval and asserts exactly one refresh.

Don't assume a coordinator's retry_after is additive to the normal interval—verify against DataUpdateCoordinator._schedule_refresh, which assigns `update_interval = self._retry_after` when set, so a short retry_after overrides a long configured interval.

When gating behavior on host hardware (e.g. total memory via os.sysconf('SC_PAGE_SIZE') * os.sysconf('SC_PHYS_PAGES')), extract the measurement into a small module-level function so tests can patch it, add an autouse fixture returning a generous default (e.g. 4 GiB) so existing tests are unaffected, and add a dedicated test for the low-resource branch plus a unit test of the measurement function itself.

Don't pick a hardware threshold equal to the documented minimum—real hosts report less than nominal (a Raspberry Pi reserves memory for the GPU), so set the cutoff below the documented spec (e.g. 1.5 GB for a 2 GB minimum) and comment why, otherwise supported devices are wrongly gated.

In Home Assistant's matter integration, zeroconf discovery during onboarding on hassio auto-installs the Matter Server add-on in the background; the config flow's async_step_zeroconf checks `not async_is_onboarded(self.hass) and is_hassio(self.hass)` before calling async_step_on_supervisor with _running_in_background=True.

When wrapping a library-specific exception (e.g. Go2RtcClientError) into HomeAssistantError, use `raise HomeAssistantError(...) from err` to preserve the cause, and add a test asserting `exc_info.value.__cause__ is <original error>` so the chaining is locked in.

When testing that a client error surfaces correctly through multiple entry points (direct helper call, HTTP proxy endpoint, service action), parametrize a fixture over the failing library method (e.g. streams.list, streams.add, get_jpeg_snapshot) and assert each path: the raised HomeAssistantError, the HTTP 500 response, and that no side effect (e.g. snapshot file) was written.

Don't let a library-specific exception escape through camera image/snapshot paths—wrap it in HomeAssistantError so the camera proxy returns a clean 500 and the snapshot service fails properly instead of producing an unhandled traceback ('Error handling request' in logs).

Don't reuse a generic/common translation key for a state whose meaning is specific to the entity (e.g. mapping an 'emergency charge control' state 'start' to the common 'start' action label) — reviewers flag that the shared label translates to the wrong wording; write an entity-specific state string (e.g. "start": "Starting") instead.

When a dependency bump's changelog adds new topics/entities, regenerate the integration's strings.json from the library's topic definitions and add a `state` map for any new enum-like topic, choosing labels that describe the state (e.g. "Starting") rather than reusing common action keys.

In Home Assistant's victron_gx integration, victron-mqtt is pinned in homeassistant/components/victron_gx/manifest.json `requirements` and mirrored in requirements_all.txt; entity names/states come from the library's topic definitions and are mirrored in strings.json under `entity` (name) and `entity.<key>.state` maps.

In Home Assistant, user-facing strings (strings.json / translations) follow sentence case: only the first word and proper nouns are capitalized (e.g. "Double press", not "Double Press"). Device trigger subtypes under `device_automation.trigger_subtype` are subject to this rule.

When sentence-casing translation strings, change only the values in strings.json (and the generated translations), leaving the keys untouched so entity/trigger identifiers and unique_ids are preserved; then grep the repo for the old capitalized strings to confirm no test or snapshot asserts on them.
Don't rename translation keys when fixing string casing—only the display values should change; renaming keys breaks entity_ids, trigger types, and existing user configurations.

When caching a parsed result keyed on an object identity (e.g. a payload object shared across subscribers), never cache mutable types like bytearray that can change in place; skip caching for those and add a dedicated test that mutates the object in place and asserts the cache is bypassed.

When adding an optional keyword-only parameter to a widely-used helper (e.g. `value_json` on Template.async_render_with_possible_json_value), use a sentinel default (e.g. `_SENTINEL`) to distinguish 'not provided' from an explicit UNDEFINED meaning 'provided but not JSON', so existing callers keep the old parse behavior unchanged.

Don't leave a per-message cache populated after the message is handled—clear it at the end of the message dispatch path (e.g. after all subscriber jobs run) so a stale parse can't be reused for a later message that happens to reuse the same object.

Don't strip or rewrite the PR template when submitting a change—keep the template structure and tick the relevant checkboxes (e.g. 'Dependency upgrade') that match the change type, since reviewers reject PRs with a removed template or unticked boxes.

When a dependency bump's release notes describe behavior fixes (e.g. sign of a negative temperature, returning None instead of a false negative), check whether the integration's consumers (sensors, binary sensors) need to handle the new None return or changed value, and note in the PR description which downstream parts depend on the bump.

When adding a code owner to an integration, update both CODEOWNERS (add /homeassistant/components/<domain>/ and /tests/components/<domain>/ lines with the GitHub handle, keeping alphabetical order) and the integration's manifest.json `codeowners` list, so the two sources stay in sync.
Don't add a code owner only to manifest.json or only to CODEOWNERS—both must be updated together, and the CODEOWNERS entries should cover both the integration directory and its tests directory.

In Home Assistant, an integration's code owners are declared in two places: the `codeowners` list in homeassistant/components/<domain>/manifest.json (GitHub handles prefixed with @) and the top-level CODEOWNERS file, which maps /homeassistant/components/<domain>/ and /tests/components/<domain>/ paths to the same handles.

When adding a new platform (e.g. light) to an integration that already has a dynamic-device listener pattern, reuse the existing `_check_device`/known_devices listener idiom from sibling platforms and gate entity creation on the device's static metadata (e.g. `primary_display_category == "LIGHT"`) rather than on live sensor values, so entities appear for all supported devices.

When mapping a 0-255 HA brightness to a device scale (e.g. 1-100), use `brightness_to_value(BRIGHTNESS_SCALE, brightness)` and `value_to_brightness(BRIGHTNESS_SCALE, value)` from homeassistant.util.color, and verify the minimum (1%) does not round to 0 on the device scale—add a test for the lowest brightness value.

Don't call the API directly from a new platform's entity methods—route every call through the integration's shared `alexa_api_call(coordinator)` (or equivalent) context manager so library errors are translated into HomeAssistantError consistently; reviewers flag direct calls that skip error handling.

When removing a deprecated/no-op API method (e.g. ConfigFlow._set_confirm_only), grep the whole repo for every call site and remove them all in one change, then turn the method into a no-op that reports usage (raising for core integrations, ignoring custom ones) so it cannot be silently reintroduced.

Don't leave the removed context key (e.g. `confirm_only` in ConfigFlowContext) defined after removing all its writers—delete the key from the TypedDict/context definition too, and grep for the key name to confirm no reader or test still references it.

In Home Assistant, `ConfigFlow._set_confirm_only()` set a `confirm_only` flag in the flow context for a frontend feature that was never built; it is unused by core and the frontend, so it is being removed from all config flows and from `ConfigFlowContext`.

When deprecating YAML import for an integration, add an `async_create_issue` call in `async_setup` (guarded by `if DOMAIN not in config: return True`) using domain HOMEASSISTANT_DOMAIN, issue_id `deprecated_yaml_{DOMAIN}`, translation_key `deprecated_yaml`, is_fixable=False, issue_domain=DOMAIN, and translation_placeholders with domain and integration_title; then add a test that sets up the component via YAML and asserts the issue exists in the issue_registry.

Don't forget to add the `deprecated_yaml` issue translation to strings.json (under `issues`) when deprecating YAML import—the issue_registry entry references translation_key `deprecated_yaml` and the placeholders domain/integration_title, so the strings must exist for the issue to render.

In Home Assistant, YAML-import deprecation issues are created in the integration's `async_setup` via `async_create_issue(hass, HOMEASSISTANT_DOMAIN, f"deprecated_yaml_{DOMAIN}", breaks_in_ha_version=..., is_fixable=False, issue_domain=DOMAIN, severity=IssueSeverity.WARNING, translation_key="deprecated_yaml", translation_placeholders={"domain": DOMAIN, "integration_title": ...})`, and tests assert on `issue_registry.async_get_issue(domain=HOMEASSISTANT_DOMAIN, issue_id=f"deprecated_yaml_{DOMAIN}")`.

When a config flow's pairing/validation loop waits on a condition that some device firmware never satisfies (e.g. a telemetry field like 'name' that older models omit), wait only on the essential condition (connection + non-empty reported state) and fall back to a sensible default for the optional field, then add a test that supplies telemetry missing that field and asserts the flow still creates the entry.

Don't cache a mutable state dictionary (e.g. `self.vacuum_state = roomba_reported_state(roomba)`) in an entity's __init__ when the library replaces that dict on each message—expose it as a @property that re-queries the library so entity properties always read live state; add a test that replaces the underlying dict after setup and asserts the entity state updates.

Don't pass a possibly-None value into a DeviceInfo field that expects a string (e.g. `name=state.get('name')`), which renders the device and all entities as 'None'; use `state.get('name') or DEFAULT_NAME` so a missing field falls back to a readable default.

Don't write tests that assert on internal implementation details (e.g. directly calling a private value_fn or checking a description's fields) when the behavior is already covered by entity-state/snapshot tests—reviewers reject such tests as 'testing an internal'; assert on the resulting entity state instead.

When adding a binary_sensor platform to an integration, define a frozen kw_only dataclass entity description with a `value_fn: Callable[[CoordinatorData], bool | None]`, gate each value on the sub-object being present (`data.state.water_flow_indicator if data.state else None`), and override `available` to return False when value_fn yields None so entities are unavailable rather than falsely off.

In Home Assistant, connectivity-style binary sensors (e.g. MQTT/Wi-Fi connected) should use BinarySensorDeviceClass.CONNECTIVITY with entity_category=EntityCategory.DIAGNOSTIC and entity_registry_enabled_default=False, since they are noise for most users; a 'water flowing' style sensor uses BinarySensorDeviceClass.RUNNING and is enabled by default.

When writing setup-error tests for an integration, parametrize a single test over all error scenarios (library API errors, BadRequestError, ClientError, TimeoutError, HTTP 500, HTTP 401) with expected ConfigEntryState and expected flow sources, rather than writing one test per error type; reviewers prefer one grouped parametrized test.

When testing that an auth failure (e.g. HTTP 401) triggers reauth, assert both the config entry state (SETUP_ERROR) and the in-progress flow sources via `[flow["context"]["source"] for flow in hass.config_entries.flow.async_progress()] == [SOURCE_REAUTH]`, while non-auth errors assert SETUP_RETRY with an empty flow list.

In Home Assistant's pterodactyl integration, setup calls `client.servers.list_servers`; PterodactylApiError/BadRequestError/ClientError/TimeoutError/HTTP 500 map to ConfigEntryState.SETUP_RETRY, while HTTP 401 triggers a reauth flow and ConfigEntryState.SETUP_ERROR.

Don't include a sentinel/unknown value (e.g. BatteryState.UNKNOWN) in a SensorDeviceClass.ENUM sensor's `options` list—map it to None in the value function instead, so the sensor reports unknown rather than a literal 'unknown' state; reviewers reject 'unknown' as an option.

When adding per-item sensors for a dynamic list of sub-devices (e.g. batteries reported by a device), build the entity descriptions from the current list at setup and register a listener that adds descriptions for items appearing later, with value functions that look the item up by name and return None when it is absent so entities go unknown while the device is away.

When adding sensors for a device's own primary resource alongside per-item sensors for the same resource type, enable the per-item sensors by default only for external/device-scope items (e.g. BatteryScope.DEVICE) and disable them for the system's own items, since the primary sensors already cover those.

When moving entities from a shared device to a new per-group/per-item device, preserve user customizations by migrating the entity registry entry's name/area_id to the new device and keeping the same unique_id so entity_ids and automations keep working; add a test that sets a custom name/area on the old entity and asserts it survives the migration.

When a new device type (e.g. a group device) is introduced, audit every device-scoped helper that assumes a real hardware device (device triggers, diagnostics, device actions, reconfigure) and add an early guard returning an empty/appropriate result for the new device type, so those features don't crash or misbehave on the synthetic device.

Don't create a synthetic device (e.g. a group device) without scoping its identifier to the config entry (e.g. `{entry_id}_group_0x{group_id:04x}`) and validating the format when parsing it back; an unscoped identifier can collide across config entries or be confused with a real device IEEE address.
